item: Seller confirms it is titled (titre foncier) and gives the title number
why: Untitled (melkia) property can be claimed by heirs and notaries will not draw the deed; 'registration in progress' (réquisition) is still open to objections. No title number, no viewing.

item: Finished with certificate of occupancy, or off-plan?
why: Off-plan means staged payments, developer risk and no ordinary mortgage; adverts with rendered images and 'livraison 20xx' are off-plan.

item: Exact building pinned on a map
why: Rental and sale comparables only mean something street by street.

item: Surface on the title (excluding terrace) confirmed
why: Adverts often add terraces; price per m² is the whole valuation method.

item: Monthly service charge (syndic) and what it covers
why: A recurring cost the advert never shows; pools, lifts and guards make it large.

item: Agent's commission agreed in writing (rate, who pays, payable only on completion)
why: Agents are unregulated and may charge both sides; whatever you sign at the viewing binds you.

item: Building rules (règlement de copropriété) allow short-term letting
why: A residence can restrict it, and the national licensing rules for private flats are unsettled — a ban ends the short-let plan.

item: Viewed in person (or by someone you trust) using the viewing checklist
why: Is it what it says it is? Photos hide damp, noise, the street and the state of the common parts.

item: Building age, structure and cracks checked; engineer's opinion if pre-2002, in the medina, or with added floors
why: Seismic rules became mandatory in 2002 and were tightened in 2013; the 2023 earthquake damaged old and earthen buildings, not modern concrete blocks.

item: Spoke to the concierge / syndic / a neighbour
why: The fastest way to learn about arrears, disputes, water pressure, noise and how many flats are already short lets.

item: Sold prices per m² gathered from several local agents
why: Adverts are asking prices. The video's method: ask 7–8 agents what similar flats actually sold for.

item: Rental evidence gathered: comparable lets and a management company's real 12-month figures
why: Occupancy drives everything, and market averages are around 40%, not the 70% often quoted.

item: Funds or mortgage agreement in principle in hand; all fees budgeted in cash
why: Fees are never financed. An agreement in principle is not binding — only the bank's written offer is.

item: Your own notary chosen and checked (Ordre des notaires directory, real office)
why: The buyer chooses and pays the notary; one you picked has no loyalty to the seller or developer.

item: Fresh ownership certificate (certificat de propriété) read by your notary
why: Shows the true owner, exact surface, mortgages, seizures and third-party claims. 100 MAD from the land registry with the title number.

item: Seller is the registered owner (all co-owners sign); any power of attorney is notarised and current
why: Forged powers of attorney and missing co-heirs are the classic routes to losing a property.

item: Certificate of occupancy / conformity (permis d'habiter) seen
why: Proof the building was lawfully completed; without it utilities, resale and lending get difficult.

item: Seller's tax clearance (quitus fiscal) for housing and communal taxes
why: The notary cannot complete without it; unpaid taxes attach to the property.

item: Syndic statement that service charges are paid up
why: By law the buyer is jointly liable for the seller's arrears.

item: Preliminary contract drawn by the notary with protective conditions; deposit held in the notary's CDG account
why: The deposit is only refundable if the contract says so: loan refusal, defective title, missing documents. Never pay a deposit to the seller or agent.

item: Full price declared in the deed and paid by bank transfer — nothing under the table
why: Undeclared cash is illegal, now attracts an extra 2% duty, cannot be repatriated, and raises your tax when you sell.

item: Purchase money sent from abroad to a convertible-dirham account; bank's foreign-currency certificates kept
why: Without proof the money came in as foreign currency, you cannot freely take the sale proceeds out again.

item: Bank's written loan offer received; 10-day reflection period respected
why: Only the written offer binds the bank (held open at least 15 days); you cannot accept before day 10.

item: Ownership certificate re-checked on the day; inventory of furniture attached; meter readings taken
why: A charge can be registered between deposit and completion; furniture you paid for must be listed to be yours.

item: Your name on the title; alerts (Mohafadati) switched on with your phone and email
why: You own it when the registry records you, not when you sign — usually 2–3 weeks later.

item: Moroccan tax adviser engaged: how the rental is declared, tax address elected, home-country reporting
why: Short-let tax treatment is unsettled and enforcement is rising; a UK resident must also report the income at home.

item: Letting set up properly: guest registration, tourist tax, insurance that covers paying guests
why: Hosts must record guests' identities; operating without the required authorisation carries fines of 50,000–500,000 MAD on paper.

item: Moroccan-notarised will covering the property
why: A foreign will is not self-executing in Morocco, and Moroccan inheritance rules apply to Moroccan nationals.
